name: Santorini
tagline: Whitewashed caldera villages above a sunken volcano.
bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep
whenBlurb: May-June and September are the honest sweet spots, warm and calmer around the caldera; July-August is beautiful but crowded, and much of the island shuts through winter.

ourTake.lede: Santorini is spectacular and oversold at once, the caldera is real, the Oia sunset scrum is not worth it. Watch the sun go down from a private terrace or a boat instead, and give the mornings to the quieter southern villages like Pyrgos and Megalochori. Come in May or late September; July and August are hot, packed and unkind to the cliff paths.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the caldera view, a cave suite and a honeymoon that photographs itself.
ourTake.skipIf: You want variety, nightlife or space away from other couples in peak season.

items.name: Sunset from the Byzantine Castle ruins of Oia
items.description: The 15th-century Venetian fortress at Oia's western tip is the island's altar to the sunset, where the sky turns from gold to rose over the caldera. It draws standing-room crowds an hour ahead, so a discreet private terrace or a chartered catamaran below often gives honeymooners the same spectacle without the elbows.

items.name: The Three Blue Domes of Oia
items.description: The trio of cobalt-domed churches stacked against the white cliff near Agios Spyridonas is the single most photographed frame in Greece. Reach the viewpoint through the alleys behind the castle at first light for the picture without a hundred phones in it.

items.name: Wander Oia's marble lanes and cliffside boutiques
items.description: Oia is a labyrinth of whitewashed cave houses, blue shutters and bougainvillea, threaded with jewellers, galleries and concept stores well suited to a slow afternoon. It is the most polished village on the island and the natural base for a multi-generation stay.

items.name: Amoudi Bay seafood tavernas below Oia
items.description: Three hundred steps drop from Oia's castle to a tiny red-cliff harbour where tavernas serve the day's catch with your feet almost in the water. Dimitris and Sunset Ammoudi will lay out grilled fish, fava and a chilled Assyrtiko; call ahead and they will happily build a full vegetarian mezze spread.

items.name: Cliff jump to the islet of Agios Nikolaos, Amoudi
items.description: Past the tavernas a dirt path leads to a rocky cove where a short swim reaches the church-topped rock of Agios Nikolaos, with a small ladder up to jumping ledges. A rite of passage for younger travellers, best done with a private boat standing by.

items.name: Fira-to-Oia caldera-edge hike
items.description: This roughly 10.5 km cliff walk runs from Fira through Firostefani and Imerovigli to Oia, hugging the caldera the whole way with the volcano always in view. Start at sunrise before the heat; a guide and a chilled hamper at the Oia end make it an event rather than a slog.

items.name: Skaros Rock and the caldera lookout
items.description: A steep footpath from Imerovigli descends to Skaros, the ruins of a 13th-century Venetian fortress on a dramatic promontory, ending at the tiny sea-facing chapel of Theoskepasti. The 360-degree caldera view is the finest on the rim and, on a clear day, reaches to Ios and Naxos.

items.name: Imerovigli, the balcony of the caldera
items.description: The highest and quietest of the caldera villages sits directly above Skaros, all serene infinity pools and unobstructed sunsets. It is where couples come to escape Oia's crush while keeping the same view, and where the island's most private suites cluster.

items.name: Akrotiri archaeological site, the Minoan Pompeii
credentials: Excavated under UNESCO-recognised Aegean Bronze Age significance
items.description: A Bronze Age town buried by the eruption around 1600 BC and preserved under ash, with three-storey houses, paved streets and sophisticated drainage under a vast climate-controlled canopy. Unlike Pompeii no bodies were found; the inhabitants seem to have fled in time, deepening the mystery. A private guide brings the frescoes-in-context to life.

items.name: Museum of Prehistoric Thera
items.description: This compact Fira museum holds the treasures lifted from Akrotiri, including the exquisite Spring Fresco and the golden ibex figurine, the finest artefacts of the lost civilisation. Pair it with the site itself for the full story of the eruption that may have seeded the Atlantis myth.

items.name: Ancient Thera on Mesa Vouno
items.description: A hilltop city founded by Dorian settlers, with Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine ruins strung along a spine 360 metres above Kamari and Perissa. Far quieter than Akrotiri, it rewards the climb with agora, theatre and temple ruins framed by sea on both sides.

items.name: Volcano hike on Nea Kameni
items.description: A short boat ride from the Old Port lands you on the black, still-steaming crater island at the caldera's heart, with a walk up to fumaroles that hiss sulphur. It is the one place you actually stand on the volcano that made Santorini.

items.name: Palea Kameni hot springs swim
items.description: Boats anchor off the older volcanic island where rust-coloured thermal water warms a small bay to a mineral bath. Wear a dark swimsuit, as the iron stains fabric; on a private charter you have the ochre cove largely to yourselves.

items.name: Private catamaran caldera cruise
items.description: A half-day sail traces the Red and White beaches, the sea caves and the Indian Rock below the Akrotiri lighthouse, with swimming and snorkelling stops and a barbecue aboard. The signature Santorini experience for couples and families alike, with the crew laying on veg-friendly mezze and Assyrtiko as the sun drops.

items.name: Sunset sail past the Akrotiri sea caves
items.description: The southwestern coast hides dark volcanic sea caves and pillar formations best seen from the water in late light. A private semi-inflatable or catamaran lets you drift into them, then hold position off Oia for the sunset from the sea, crowd-free.

items.name: Akrotiri Lighthouse (Faros)
items.description: Built by a French company in 1892, this working lighthouse on the island's southwestern cape is one of the oldest in Greece and a serene, near-empty alternative to Oia for sunset. There is no crowd, no ticket, just the red sun sinking into the Aegean from the low stone wall.

items.name: Red Beach at Akrotiri
items.description: A crescent of dark sand beneath towering blood-red volcanic cliffs, one of the most striking shorelines in Greece. Be honest with expectations: the cliff path has been officially closed for rockfall risk since 2013, with major slides as recently as 2025, so the safe way to see it now is by boat from the water.

items.name: White Beach by boat
items.description: Just south of Red Beach, pale chalk-white cliffs rise over dark pebbles in a cove reachable only by sea. Catamarans stop here to swim and snorkel; the colour contrast against the caldera water is extraordinary.

items.name: Perivolos black-sand beach and beach clubs
items.description: The long southern stretch beyond Perissa is Santorini's chic beach-club scene, where organised loungers, cocktails and DJ sets meet volcanic black sand. The polished end of the island's beach life for a relaxed, well-served day.

items.name: Perissa Beach under Mesa Vouno
items.description: A broad sweep of jet-black sand at the foot of the Ancient Thera mountain, with tavernas, watersports and warm shallow water. Family-friendly and less styled than Perivolos, good for an easy multi-generation day by the sea.

items.name: Kamari Beach and its promenade
items.description: The island's most established black-sand resort beach, with a palm-lined seafront of restaurants and cafes under the cliff of Mesa Vouno. Convenient, walkable and calm, it suits families who want the beach and dinner in one place.

items.name: Vlychada Beach and its sculpted cliffs
items.description: Wind and water have carved the pale volcanic cliffs above this southern beach into lunar, almost gallery-like forms. Quieter and more space than the busier beaches, with a smart marina taverna scene for a slow lunch.

items.name: Santo Wines caldera tasting
items.description: The island's grower cooperative sits on the caldera edge near Pyrgos with a sweeping terrace, making it the classic first Assyrtiko tasting with the volcano in front of you. Book a private flight at golden hour, when the setting does as much as the wine.

items.name: Venetsanos Winery above Athinios port
items.description: One of the island's oldest wineries, from 1947, is dug dramatically into the cliff above the ferry port, with a gravity-flow cellar and a knife-edge terrace. Its naturally vinified Assyrtiko and the architecture make it a favourite for a refined sunset tasting.

items.name: Domaine Sigalas near Oia
credentials: Internationally acclaimed Assyrtiko producer
items.description: Paris Sigalas's estate on the fertile northern plain is widely held to make some of the finest single-varietal Assyrtiko in Greece, in a relaxed garden setting away from the cliff crowds. A serious tasting with vine-side food pairings, and easy to reach from Oia.

items.name: Estate Argyros and its 150-year-old vines
credentials: Internationally awarded; among Santorini's oldest vines
items.description: Founded in 1903 and now in its fourth generation, Argyros farms some of the oldest ungrafted Assyrtiko vines on earth and is a benchmark for age-worthy Santorini wine and Vinsanto. The premium flight is the collector's stop on any wine day.

items.name: Koutsoyannopoulos Wine Museum
items.description: A wine cellar carved eight metres underground tells the story of Santorini winemaking through animated tableaux, ending in a tasting. A cool, unhurried hour that suits a hot afternoon and travellers who want the context before the estates.

items.name: Pyrgos village and the Kasteli
items.description: The best-preserved of the island's Venetian castle-villages spirals up to a hilltop Kasteli with over-the-rooftops views across all of Santorini. Its dozens of tiny churches and near-empty lanes make it the antidote to Oia, and a lovely, crowd-free sunset.

items.name: Monastery of Profitis Ilias
items.description: The island's highest point at 565 metres carries an 18th-century monastery with a small museum of icons and relics and the widest panorama on Santorini. On a clear day the whole caldera and neighbouring islands lay out below you.

items.name: Megalochori, the vineyard village
items.description: A genuinely lived-in village of arched lanes, bell towers and cave houses set among vineyards, largely untouched by mass tourism. Wine estates ring it, and its quiet squares make an atmospheric, unhurried dinner spot.

items.name: Emporio and its medieval Kasteli
items.description: The island's largest village hides a labyrinthine fortified quarter, the Kasteli, whose windowless outer houses once formed a defensive wall against pirates. Wandering its shaded maze is a rare glimpse of everyday Cycladic life beyond the postcard villages.

items.name: Thirassia island day trip
items.description: Across the caldera lies Santorini's sleepy sibling, reached by boat to Korfos harbour, where waterfront tavernas serve honest grilled fish and fava with the caldera as backdrop. Climb the steps or path to Manolas village for a 360-degree view and a taste of the islands fifty years ago; bring cash, as cards often don't work.

items.name: Fira Old Port and the cable car
items.description: A three-minute cable-car ride drops from Fira to the Old Port of Gialos more than 200 metres below, the graceful alternative to the 588 zigzag steps. From the port, private boats and cruise tenders set off across the caldera.

items.name: Three Bells of Fira (Catholic Church of the Dormition)
items.description: The blue-domed church with its three white bell arches framing the caldera is among the most photographed spots in Fira. Set on the town's northern edge toward Firostefani, it catches beautiful light in the late afternoon.

items.name: Firostefani, the crown of Fira
items.description: A short caldera walk from Fira's bustle, this calmer village offers the same jaw-dropping volcano views with a fraction of the crowd. It is a refined base for those who want to walk to Fira's restaurants yet sleep in quiet.

items.name: Atlantis Books
items.description: A cult independent bookshop founded by a group of friends, now on the Firostefani cliffs, warren-like and stacked with rare and secondhand titles in many languages. A cool, cultured retreat and a genuinely different souvenir for the reader in the family.

items.name: Fira's caldera-edge galleries and boutiques
items.description: The capital's cliff lanes are lined with jewellers, art galleries and designer boutiques catching sea views between the whitewashed walls. The most concentrated shopping on the island, and a pleasant way to fill the hours before the sunset.

items.name: Cine Kamari open-air cinema
credentials: Named among the world's best open-air cinemas by CNN, The Guardian and Travel Channel
items.description: Since 1987 this garden cinema at the edge of Kamari has screened films under the stars with a drink in hand, a quintessential Greek-summer evening. It runs May to October, an unexpectedly romantic close to a beach day.

items.name: Tomato Industrial Museum, Vlychada
items.description: Housed in the old D. Nomikos tomato-processing factory, this museum tells the story of the island's once-vital tomato industry through machinery, oral histories and art, and hosts the Santorini Film Festival. A thoughtful, offbeat stop on the quiet south coast.

items.name: Santorini Arts Factory events
items.description: The same restored Vlychada factory complex doubles as the island's leading cultural venue, staging exhibitions, concerts and the summer film festival under the stars. Worth checking the programme for a cultured evening away from the caldera crowds.

items.name: Village churches and bell towers of Megalochori
items.description: Two grand freestanding bell towers and a scatter of blue-domed chapels give this vineyard village a photogenic, deeply local character. A slow morning here, cameras in hand, is a quieter counterpart to Oia's dome-hunting.

items.name: Sunrise over the caldera from Imerovigli
items.description: Everyone chases the sunset; the smarter luxury is the sunrise, when the caldera glows pink and the villages are silent. From an Imerovigli terrace or a private plunge pool it is the island's most intimate hour, and the one no crowd will share.

items.description: Fish by the kilo at the water's edge below Oia, the day's catch, grilled, with your feet almost in the Aegean.

items.name: Roka

items.name: PK Cocktail Bar

items.description: Terraces cascading down the Fira cliff, each with an unbroken caldera view, the island's best-known sunset bar for half a century.

items.name: Franco's Bar
credentials: A long-standing Fira caldera institution, classical music at sunset
items.description: A caldera-path institution where classical music plays the sun down, a decades-old ritual of a Santorini evening.

items.name: V Lounge
credentials: A noted Fira caldera-view cocktail lounge
items.description: A calmer caldera-view lounge on the Fira cliff, considered cocktails and room to breathe, away from the sunset scrum.

items.name: Lure
credentials: Part of the Andronis collection, Small Luxury Hotels of the World

items.description: Andronis' cliff-top rooftop above Oia, fine dining and serious mixology on Greek herbs and botanicals, with the caldera below.

plan.heading: 3 days in Santorini, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A slow morning on your suite terrace at Katikies or Canaves, the caldera dropping away below.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The quiet end of Oia's marble lanes, the Atlantis bookshop, and the old castle ruin.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: The sunset from a private terrace, then dinner at Lycabettus above Oia's cliff.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private catamaran from Ammoudi around the caldera to the hot springs and Thirassia.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch aboard at anchor, then a swim off the red and white volcanic beaches.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Grilled fish at the Ammoudi Bay tavernas, boats knocking at the jetty beside you.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Akrotiri excavations, the Bronze Age city preserved under ash, then Santo Wines' assyrtiko.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A tasting flight and lunch on the caldera terrace at a family estate in Pyrgos.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Selene in Pyrgos, the island's serious kitchen, well away from the crowds.

items.name: Oia
items.description: The famous cliff village, beautiful but crowded; best for a splurge suite, not a base for exploring.

items.name: Imerovigli
items.description: Quieter caldera-edge village with the best views, the calm luxury base.

items.name: Pyrgos / Megalochori
items.description: Inland stone villages away from the crowds, for authenticity over the sunset postcard.

events.name: Santorini Experience
events.note: An open-water swim and running event set against the caldera, at the season's gentler end.

events.name: Ifestia Festival
events.note: A re-enactment of the volcano's eruption with fireworks over the caldera at Fira.

events.name: Greek Orthodox Easter
events.note: Candlelit processions and fireworks in the villages, the islands' most moving celebration; date follows the Orthodox calendar.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Imerovigli or Oia for the quietest caldera views away from the cruise-day crowds in Fira; book sunset dinners well ahead, and note that many cave suites reach the pool by steps, not lifts.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Santorini (JTR) or transfer by private helicopter or seaplane from Athens; a car meets you and climbs to the caldera villages, or arrive by private yacht into the old port.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver, as the cliff roads are narrow and parking scarce; Oia and Fira themselves are walked on stepped lanes, so pack for cobbles rather than heels.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is good across the island and an eSIM works well; villa and hotel wifi is reliable despite the terrain.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro; cards are accepted throughout, some cash helps in smaller tavernas, and rounding up is the customary tip.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late May-June and September give warm sun, calm seas and unbroken caldera light; July-August is hot and heavily crowded, and winter (Nov-Mar) sees many hotels and restaurants shut.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Reach it via Athens, no India nonstop. Fly into Athens (IndiGo direct, or a Gulf/Turkish hub in business), then a 45-minute Aegean/Sky Express hop to Santorini (JTR), or a private transfer to a Piraeus seat on a high-speed ferry. Book the Athens-Santorini leg early in summer; a same-airport Aegean connection is the cleanest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed; mainland-supplied bottled water is standard as the island's tap water is desalinated and brackish, drink bottled. Very safe; the real hazards are steep, uneven caldera steps and cliff paths. No altitude issue.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Manageable for vegetarians, Santorinian tomatoes, fava and white aubergine are local specialities; Jain requires clear briefing and advance notice. Indian food is scarce, so a villa chef is worth arranging; Metaxi Mas and Selene do fine vegetable-led menus.
